activities.anchor: The claims are testable, because constituents behave as units
activities.caption: pair each diagnostic with what it shows
activities.name: synConstitMatch

config.prompt: Four diagnostics, one hidden tree — pair each with its demonstration:

pairs.right: the string behaves as one unit
the phrase fronts as one piece

pairs.left: coordination — [the dog] and [the cat] joined with 'and'

pairs.right: the whole phrase moves to ask about it

config.why: Run on any sentence, the diagnostics reveal the hidden tree without any theory loaded in advance.

activities.anchor: Same string, different trees, different meanings
activities.caption: find the line the parse refuses
activities.name: synAmbigSpot

config.prompt: One line of this ambiguity report is wrong — click it:
lines: 'I saw the man with the telescope' has two parses over one string.
The prepositional phrase can attach to 'saw' — the instrument reading.
The ear picks one parse and locks it permanently.
Headlines mine the seam: 'Squad Helps Dog Bite Victim'.
config.correction: The ear flickers between them — the ambiguity lives in the structure, not in any single word.
config.why: Ambiguity that survives word-by-word paraphrase is the proof that structure is real.

activities.anchor: that example is already at the edge
activities.caption: drop the marker on comprehension's ceiling
activities.name: synNestPlace

config.prompt: 'The cat [the dog [the man owned] chased] ran' is already at the edge. After roughly how many nestings does English comprehension give out?
config.why: Two — but that is memory, not grammar: the rule system itself places no ceiling on depth. Recursion is what makes language productive — indefinitely many sentences nobody has ever said before.

activities.anchor: The same machinery explains dependencies at distance
activities.caption: true or false — key versus cabinets
activities.name: synAgreeJudge

statements.s: In 'The key to the cabinets is on the table', the verb agrees with 'key', not the nearer 'cabinets'.
statements.why: Agreement tracks the structural head — exactly what a tree encodes and a string does not.
If it did, 'is' would be 'are' — the string picture fails.

statements.s: Children make agreement errors with local nouns ('agreement attraction') — evidence that even immature grammars compute structure.
statements.why: The errors are structure-shaped, not string-shaped.

statements.s: A list of word-order habits could explain the agreement.
statements.why: Some machinery is tracking structure, not linear neighbours — the tree is that machinery made visible.

activities.anchor: Questions expose the tree even more sharply
activities.caption: run the movement derivation in order
activities.name: synMoveOrder

config.prompt: From statement to question — order the derivation:
items: 'what' starts as the object of eat — compare 'You ate what'
the question word moves from its argument position to the front
the grammar tracks the launch site and the landing site — a gap after the verb
config.why: Passives work the same way ('The cat was chased' — the object became the subject); relative clauses and whole-clause questions inherit the machinery.

activities.anchor: The expert payoff is that movement is
activities.caption: try to build the question — hit the barrier
activities.name: synIslandBranch

config.root: You want to ask about the thing Mary ate — but it sits inside a clause you are already wondering about.

start.text: Assemble the question. What do you get?

choices.label: 'What do you wonder whether Mary ate?'
choices.feedback: It collapses — elements cannot cross certain structural barriers.

choices.label: Question within the main clause instead
choices.feedback: Movement within its own clause is fine — the barriers are structural, not distance-based.

collapse.text: The 'island' constraints: no teacher shows you them, yet every speaker respects them without knowing they exist.

fine.text: 'What did you eat?'-style movement launches and lands inside one clause — universal, unlearned, exceptionless.

choices.label: Now try crossing into the embedded question anyway

config.why: Universal and unlearned constraints — the evidence pattern that launched the generative programme, and the reason syntax became linguistics' most theory-driven branch.

activities.anchor: Verbs determine what can follow them
activities.caption: file each verb by its appetite
activities.name: synAppetiteBuckets

config.prompt: The trees record the demands — file each verb:

items.label: devour — 'The dragon devoured the village', never 'The dragon devoured'
put — it demands an object and a location ('put it there')
eat — can drop its object when the meal is understood

config.why: Every speaker commands thousands of these verb-specific requirements without instruction — and the classic tacit-knowledge pair: 'The cat seems sleeping' is out, 'The cat seems to be sleeping' is fine.

activities.anchor: Movement is not the only way to build a question
activities.caption: drag the divider — move it or leave it in place
activities.name: synInSituCompare

config.prompt: One computation, two strategies — drag the divider:

before.label: English — move the question word
before.text: 'What did you eat?' — fronted, with a gap after the verb; islands only exist in languages that move at all.

after.label: Mandarin & Japanese — wh-in-situ
after.text: 'Nǐ chī shénme' — literally 'you eat what': the word stays where the missing argument belongs; Japanese adds a sentence-final particle.

config.why: In both, 'what' must be understood as the object of 'eat', and both respect locality the same way — the tree with its argument positions is the deep object; the linear order is a variable surface convention.
